subtype: Approach: making many complicated rules before playing [Pitfall]
passage: Last summer I invented a game called Fort Attack, and I wanted it to be perfect. So before anyone played, I sat on the steps and wrote rules. Where the fort is. How many guards. What happens if you're caught twice. What happens if it rains. By the time Harsha and the others came down, I had twenty rules on two pages. I started reading them out. At rule seven, Harsha was picking at a scab. At rule twelve, two of them were whispering. At rule sixteen, Harsha said, 'Yash bhai, what was rule three again?' I didn't know either. When I finished, they'd already gone to play cricket. I sat there holding my two perfect pages.

qa.q: How many rules did Yash write?
qa.a: Twenty rules on two pages.

qa.q: How did Yash feel holding his pages at the end?
qa.a: Yash probably felt disappointed and a bit foolish, left alone with rules nobody wanted to play.

qa.q: What would you change first in Yash's approach?
qa.a: Write only three or four key rules, play a quick round, and add more only when a problem comes up.

qa.q: What was listening to the rules like for Harsha?
qa.a: Harsha got bored, picking at a scab and forgetting rule three, and chose cricket instead.

grounding: Shows a boy writing twenty rules before anyone plays, so his friends lose interest, forget the rules and drift off to another game.

subtype: Approach: making many complicated rules before playing [Pitfall]
passage: Camp leader's log, day 3. At free-play time, Amandeep offered to invent a game for his group. He spent the first fifteen minutes writing rules in his notebook and then read them aloud: twenty of them, with sub-rules. Bidisha asked two questions about rule five; by rule fourteen she was drawing on her hand. Two boys wandered off to the swings. When he said, 'Okay, let's start!', only three children were left, and none of them remembered the rules. He looked crushed. Tomorrow I'll suggest he try three rules and a trial round, and add more only when needed.

qa.q: How long did Amandeep spend writing rules?
qa.a: The first fifteen minutes of free-play time.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when only three children were left?
qa.a: He looked crushed, so he felt deeply disappointed that his careful rules had driven the group away.

qa.q: What does the note-writer plan to suggest, and why could it work?
qa.a: Three rules and a trial round, adding more only when needed, so people start playing before they lose interest.

qa.q: How did Bidisha experience the reading of the rules?
qa.a: Bidisha was interested at first, asking about rule five, but by rule fourteen she was bored and drawing on her hand.

grounding: Illustrates a boy writing twenty complicated rules before play, while the group loses interest, forgets them and drifts away.

subtype: Approach: changing rules in the middle to win [Pitfall]
passage: I learned this one the hard way, last Diwali holiday. We were playing a board game I'd made up, with dice and paper coins. Every time Uma was about to win, I'd think of a new rule. 'Oh, landing on red means go back five.' 'Oh, you need a six to finish.' The first time, she laughed. The second time, she frowned. The third time, she put down the dice and said, 'Zubin bhai, you're just changing it so you win.' My cousin nodded. They both went to the balcony and started a card game without me. I sat there with my board, my new rules and nobody to play with. A game with moving rules isn't a game.

qa.q: What was the new rule about landing on red?
qa.a: Landing on red means go back five.

qa.q: How did Uma feel by the third new rule?
qa.a: Uma felt cheated and fed up, putting down the dice and saying he was changing the rules to win.

qa.q: What should Zubin do next time he wants a new rule?
qa.a: Suggest it before the next game starts, not in the middle of one, so everyone agrees and the rules stay fixed while playing.

qa.q: How might Zubin's cousin have seen the game?
qa.a: The cousin nodded along with Uma, so the cousin also seemed to find the game unfair and chose cards instead.

grounding: Shows a child adding new rules whenever he is about to lose, until the others feel cheated and leave him alone.

subtype: Approach: changing rules in the middle to win [Pitfall]
passage: PT teacher's note, Thursday. During free games, Joseph's group played a tagging game he had set up. Twice, when he was about to be caught, he announced a new rule: first 'the tree is safe', then 'you can't tag anyone wearing blue', and he was wearing blue. Kamal said, 'That's not fair, you're changing it to win,' and walked off. Three more followed. Joseph was left standing by the tree, calling after them. I talked with him afterwards. He said, quietly, 'It's not fun alone.' We agreed that new rules can only start from the next game.

qa.q: What was the second new rule Joseph announced?
qa.a: 'You can't tag anyone wearing blue', and he was wearing blue.

qa.q: How did Joseph seem to feel when he said 'It's not fun alone'?
qa.a: He seemed lonely and a little ashamed, realising the changed rules had cost him his friends' company.

qa.q: How does the agreed rule help?
qa.a: It keeps rules fixed while a game is being played, with new ones starting only from the next game, so nobody feels cheated.

qa.q: How did Kamal see Joseph's new rules?
qa.a: Kamal felt they were unfair tricks to win, so he said so and walked off.

grounding: Illustrates a boy changing the rules mid-game whenever he is about to lose, until the others feel cheated and leave.

subtype: Approach: agreeing rules together before starting [Action]
passage:
Monday. Darshan's cricket-and-tag game in the colony park ended after ten minutes, with Wasim and two others shouting that nobody had agreed anything.
Wednesday. Before playing, Darshan got all six of them to sit in a circle on the grass. 'Each person says one rule.' Wasim: 'No hitting the ball into the road.' Someone else: 'Out if caught one-handed off the wall.' That one started a fight, so they voted: four to two. Darshan wrote all six on the back of a chart paper and taped it to the bench.
Friday. Wasim's shot bounced off the wall into a fielder's hand. 'Out!' 'Not out!' Everyone turned to the chart. Rule four. Wasim groaned, grinned, and handed over his bat.

qa.q: How did the vote on the wall rule go?
qa.a: Four to two.

qa.q: How did Wasim seem to feel when the chart showed he was out?
qa.a: He groaned but grinned, so he seemed disappointed yet accepting, since everyone had agreed the rule.

qa.q: What else could make the chart even more useful?
qa.a: A line saying how new rules get added, so changes also go through the circle and a vote.

qa.q: What might the change from Monday to Friday be like for the rest of the group?
qa.a: Instead of a game ending in shouting after ten minutes, they keep playing, because disagreements are settled by the chart.

grounding: Shows a group sitting in a circle, each suggesting one rule, voting on a disagreement, and writing the final list on a chart to prevent later arguments.

subtype: Approach: agreeing rules together before starting [Action]
passage: Usha, your friends keep fighting over rules? Your Reena Masi learned a trick at your age. Every Sunday we played a big chasing game in the mohalla, and every Sunday it broke up in a fight. One day our neighbour's eldest girl made us all sit in a circle on the temple steps. 'Each one, one rule.' We gave nine rules. Two of them clashed, so we voted with our hands up. Then she wrote the final list on the back of an old calendar in thick charcoal and hung it on the gate. After that, whenever someone shouted 'Not fair!', we just pointed at the calendar. No more fights. Well, fewer.

qa.q: Where did they hang the list of rules?
qa.a: On the gate, written on the back of an old calendar in thick charcoal.

qa.q: How did young Reena feel about the Sunday games before the circle?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated, since every Sunday the game broke up in a fight.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the games calmer?
qa.a: Sitting in a circle so each child gave one rule, voting on the ones that clashed, and posting the list where everyone could see it.

qa.q: How did the neighbour's eldest girl seem to see the fights?
qa.a: She seemed fed up enough to organise everyone, and practical, turning the fights into a voting circle and a posted list.

grounding: Illustrates children sitting in a circle, each giving a rule, voting on clashes and writing the final list up so nobody argues later.

subtype: Approach: adapting the game for the youngest player [Revision]
passage:
"Got you, Chiku! Out!"
"Again?" Our six-year-old cousin Chiku sat down on the step, and his chin started to wobble.
"Third time," Kavitha whispered to Yamini. "He's going to cry."
He did, loudly.
"Stop the game," Yamini called. "Wait. He's always out first because he's slow."
"So he should practise running," said Kavitha.
"He's six! What if... the mat by the door is a safe zone. Only for little ones. Nobody can catch them there."
"Only for him?"
"For anyone under eight."
Chiku wiped his face. "I can stand on the mat?"
"As long as you want. But you have to run to it."
Chiku ran to the mat and stood there, beaming. The game started again, with everyone still in.

qa.q: How many times had Chiku been out?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: How did Chiku feel once he could stand on the mat?
qa.a: He beamed, so he felt happy and safe after crying about being out 😊

qa.q: What else could make the game fair for Chiku?
qa.a: A head start or a partner, while checking the safe zone doesn't make it too easy; noticing the crying and changing a rule is what kept him in.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see the new rule at first?
qa.a: Kavitha thinks Chiku should just practise running and asks 'Only for him?', so Kavitha is unsure it's fair at first.

grounding: Shows older children noticing their six-year-old cousin keeps getting out first and crying, and adding a safe zone so everyone stays in.

subtype: Approach: adapting the game for the youngest player [Revision]
passage: At Nani's house last summer, we played catch in the courtyard every evening, and my six-year-old cousin Chandrika was always out first. On the third evening she sat down by the tulsi pot and cried so hard she got hiccups. At first I thought, that's how the game works. Then I looked at her tiny legs next to ours and thought: this isn't a game for her; it's just losing. So I told the others, 'The charpai is a safe zone for anyone under eight. Nobody can catch you there.' Chandrika stopped hiccuping. She ran to the charpai, then off again, laughing, then back. She stayed in the game until Nani called, 'Lalit, Chandrika, dinner!'

qa.q: Where did Chandrika sit and cry?
qa.a: By the tulsi pot.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he looked at Chandrika's legs?
qa.a: Lalit felt sorry for her, seeing that for someone so small the game was 'just losing'.

qa.q: Why was the safe zone a good fix?
qa.a: It let Chandrika stay in without spoiling the game for the older children, since she still had to run to reach the charpai.

qa.q: How did the new rule change the evening for Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika went from crying with hiccups to laughing and running, staying in the game until dinner.

grounding: Illustrates older children seeing a six-year-old cousin always out first and in tears, and adding a safe zone so she can stay in the game.

subtype: Approach: thinking what would spoil the game and blocking it [Thinking]
passage: Before the hide-and-seek game behind the panchayat hall, Payal held up her hand. "Wait. What could spoil this?" The others groaned, but Hansa said, "Last time Munna hid in the sugarcane and nobody found him till dark." Payal nodded. "So hiding places that go on forever make it endless. And boring for the seeker." She picked up a lump of chalk from the school step and drew a line around the hall, the neem tree and the well. "Nobody hides past this line. And if you're not found in two minutes, you come out yourself." Hansa counted the seconds on her fingers. The first round took less than five minutes, and everyone got a turn to seek.

qa.q: Where did Munna hide last time?
qa.a: In the sugarcane; nobody found him till dark.

qa.q: Why did Payal hold up her hand before the game?
qa.a: She was worried the game might be spoiled again and felt determined to think it through first so it would be fair.

qa.q: What else might spoil the game that Payal could plan for?
qa.a: Someone peeking while counting; asking 'what could spoil this?' beforehand lets them fix problems before they happen.

qa.q: How does Hansa see Payal's question?
qa.a: Hansa takes it seriously, remembering Munna in the sugarcane, and even helps by counting the seconds.

grounding: Shows a girl asking what could spoil a hide-and-seek game, seeing endless hiding places are the problem, and setting a two-minute limit and a chalk boundary.

subtype: Approach: thinking what would spoil the game and blocking it [Thinking]
passage: On their estate in Nairobi, Esther and Wanjiru gathered seven kids for hide-and-seek. Before anyone ran, Esther sat on the wall and thought aloud. "What could ruin this? What would make it dull?" Wanjiru shrugged. "Someone hiding in the next block, so we search forever." "Right," said Esther. "Endless hiding spots, endless game." She borrowed pink chalk from a little one and drew a line from the water tank to the gate. "Inside this line only. And the seeker gets two minutes. If you're not found by then, you win the round and come out." The first seeker found four in two minutes. Nobody wandered to the next block, and they played until the streetlights came on.

qa.q: Where did Esther draw the chalk line?
qa.a: From the water tank to the gate.

qa.q: Why did Esther sit on the wall and think aloud before playing?
qa.a: She was concerned the game could turn unfair or boring, and felt calm and curious enough to prevent it rather than rushing in.

qa.q: What else could Esther's group ask before their next game?
qa.a: Whether the smallest kids have a fair chance, using the same 'what would spoil it?' question to fix problems early.

qa.q: How might the younger kids on the estate experience the new rules?
qa.a: Nobody vanishes to the next block and rounds end quickly, so they get to keep playing until the streetlights come on.

grounding: Illustrates a girl asking what would make a game unfair or boring, blocking endless hiding with a two-minute limit and a chalk boundary.

subtype: Approach: using scraps to build the game pieces [Action]
passage:
Friday. Rain again, and the only board game in the flat was missing half its pieces. Payal and her cousin Deepika sat on the floor, bored.
Saturday. They got to work. Deepika cut two empty cereal boxes into cards and wrote a city on each: Kolkata, Jaipur, Kochi, Guwahati. Payal drew a map of India on old chart paper and dotted a railway line between the cities. Four bottle caps from the kitchen became tokens.
Sunday. The game was called 'Train Across India'. Roll the dice, pick a card, move your cap to that city. Payal reached Kochi first, but Deepika demanded a rematch, and Payal's little brother begged to join.

qa.q: What became the tokens?
qa.a: Four bottle caps from the kitchen.

qa.q: How did Payal and Deepika feel on Friday?
qa.a: They were bored, stuck indoors with a board game missing half its pieces.

qa.q: What made their approach work?
qa.a: Using what they had, boxes, chart paper and caps, instead of waiting for a proper board game.

qa.q: How does Payal's little brother see the new game?
qa.a: He begs to join, so the home-made game seems exciting to him 😊

grounding: Shows children with no usable board game making cards from cereal boxes and tokens from bottle caps to invent a game about travelling across India.

subtype: Approach: using scraps to build the game pieces [Action]
passage: Samir, bored because the tablet's charging? When your Grandma Elizabeth was your age in Shillong, we didn't even have a proper board game. So one monsoon, my brother and I made our own. We cut up old cereal boxes into cards and wrote the names of places on them: Delhi, Madras, Bombay, Calcutta, our own Shillong. Bottle caps were our tokens, one green, one red. The board was a map of India I traced from my school atlas. Each card said where your train went next, and some said 'Train late, miss a turn'. We played it all through the rains. Your great-uncle cheated terribly, but we still played.

qa.q: What did some of the cards say?
qa.a: 'Train late, miss a turn'.

qa.q: How does Grandma Elizabeth seem to feel about the home-made game?
qa.a: She seems proud and fond of it, remembering playing it all through the rains.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the game possible?
qa.a: Using what they already had, cereal boxes, bottle caps and a traced map, instead of wishing for a proper board game.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth's brother take part in the game?
qa.a: He played all through the rains too, though she says he cheated terribly, which she remembers with amusement.

grounding: Illustrates children making a travelling-across-India game from cut cereal boxes and bottle caps because they had no board game.

subtype: Approach: letting the loudest member decide [Pitfall]
passage: In their classroom in Stockholm, four children bent over a big sheet for the solar system chart. Oskar grabbed the markers. "Sun in the middle, planets in a line, biggest to smallest. My way." Tomas opened his mouth. "Could we add the moons? Jupiter has loads." Oskar was already drawing. "No room." The two girls at the end exchanged a look and stopped offering ideas. By the end of the lesson, Oskar had coloured every planet himself. Tomas was doodling tiny moons in the margin of his notebook, where nobody would see them. When the teacher asked the group what they'd learned, only Oskar answered.

qa.q: What did Tomas want to add to the chart?
qa.a: The moons, since Jupiter has loads.

qa.q: What does Tomas doodling moons in his notebook suggest?
qa.a: He felt shut out and discouraged, keeping his idea where nobody would see it after Oskar said there was no room.

qa.q: What could the group have done so all four were heard?
qa.a: Take turns suggesting one idea each before anyone draws, then decide together; letting the loudest decide lost the moons.

qa.q: How did the chart work look to the two girls at the end?
qa.a: They exchanged a look and stopped offering ideas, so they seem to have lost interest and felt their voices didn't count.

grounding: Shows a group of four where one boy insists on his chart design, the others go quiet and lose interest, and ideas like adding moons never appear.

subtype: Approach: letting the loudest member decide [Pitfall]
passage: In the school library, Thomas, Maria, Irfan and Keya had one period to plan their solar system chart. Thomas spoke first and didn't stop. "Black background. Planets in a curve. I'll draw Saturn, it's the coolest." Maria had a sheet of her own notes, with the moons of each planet counted in pencil. She slid it across. Thomas glanced at it. "Too messy. Just planets." Irfan stopped suggesting after that. Keya went to look at books. Maria folded her sheet back into her bag. On submission day the chart was neat and bare. The teacher wrote: 'Good, but where are the moons?' Maria looked at her bag and said nothing.

qa.q: What did the teacher write on the chart?
qa.a: 'Good, but where are the moons?'

qa.q: What might Maria have felt when the teacher asked about the moons?
qa.a: She likely felt a quiet sting of frustration, since the moons were in her folded notes all along.

qa.q: What else could Maria try next time her idea is brushed aside?
qa.a: Ask the group to hear each person's idea first, or ask the teacher to help set turns, so quieter ideas reach the chart.

qa.q: How did Thomas's way of deciding affect Irfan and Keya?
qa.a: Irfan stopped suggesting and Keya wandered off to the books, so both lost interest in the project.

grounding: Illustrates the loudest member of a group of four deciding the chart alone, so quieter members lose interest and their idea of adding moons is lost.

subtype: Approach: listing everyone's ideas and voting [Thinking]
passage:
"We've argued for twenty minutes," said Jaya. "Let's do it properly. Everyone writes their idea on a strip."
Zeenat tore a page into four. "Model volcano." "Chart of rocks." "A short play about an earthquake." "Quiz game."
"Now each of us gets two votes. Tick any two strips, but not your own twice."
Pencils scratched.
"Volcano: four. Play: three. Quiz: one. Chart: zero."
"The chart was mine," said Zeenat quietly.
Jaya looked at her. "Can the volcano have a chart next to it, explaining the layers? You're the best at labels."
Zeenat thought, then half-smiled. "Okay. But I'm doing the lava colours too."

qa.q: How many votes did the volcano get?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel when her chart got no votes?
qa.a: Zeenat felt disappointed, saying quietly that the chart was hers.

qa.q: What did Jaya do well after the vote, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She found a place for Zeenat's skill in the winning idea, labels beside the volcano, so the vote didn't leave Zeenat out.

qa.q: How might the rest of the group see the voting?
qa.a: Everyone got two votes and a say, so the result felt fair even to those whose ideas lost.

grounding: Shows a group writing each child's idea on a strip and voting twice each, giving everyone a say though one idea's owner feels disappointed.

subtype: Approach: listing everyone's ideas and voting [Thinking]
passage: Our group of five had argued for three days about the science fair. Everyone thought their own idea was best, and I was tired of it. Then I remembered how my class elects the monitor. At lunch I said, 'Let's each write our idea on a paper strip, and everyone gets two votes.' We had five strips: water filter, solar oven, plant growth, rain gauge, magnet car. I wanted the magnet car. Alka's water filter got five votes; my car got two. I felt a pinch, honestly. But nobody could say it wasn't fair, because everyone had voted. And by Friday we'd built the filter, instead of still arguing. Alka said, 'Nitin, you can do the testing.'

qa.q: Which idea did Nitin want?
qa.a: The magnet car.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel when the magnet car got two votes?
qa.a: Nitin felt a pinch of disappointment, but accepted it because the vote was fair.

qa.q: Why did voting work better than three days of arguing?
qa.a: Everyone had a say, so nobody could call the result unfair, and the group could finally start building.

qa.q: How might Alka see the vote?
qa.a: Alka's water filter won with five votes, so Alka likely felt pleased and valued, and gave Nitin the testing to do.

grounding: Illustrates a group writing every idea on paper strips and giving each member two votes, which feels fair even to the child whose idea loses.

subtype: Approach: mixing two ideas into one plan [Thinking]
passage: The windmill project was due in two days, and the group was split down the middle. Shreya and Kiran wanted a model; Tushar and Anjali wanted a poster. They had one evening and only the materials in Shreya's house. "A model looks better," Kiran said. "A poster explains more," said Tushar. Shreya stared at the chart paper and the ice-cream sticks on the floor. "What if... it's a poster, with all the explaining, and a small windmill stuck on it that really turns?" Tushar tilted his head. "Only small?" "Palm-sized. Pinned in the corner." By nine the poster was done, and when you blew on the corner, the little windmill spun.

qa.q: What was the project about?
qa.a: Windmills.

qa.q: What was Shreya thinking as she stared at the chart paper and sticks?
qa.a: She was looking for a way to satisfy both halves, and felt hopeful when the idea of a poster with a small windmill came.

qa.q: Why did mixing the ideas work better than choosing one?
qa.a: Both pairs kept what they cared about, the explaining and the moving model, so nobody felt they had lost.

qa.q: How might Tushar see the final poster?
qa.a: Tushar wanted a poster that explains and got one, with a little windmill he could accept, so he'd likely be satisfied.

grounding: Shows a split group combining ideas into a poster with a small turning windmill attached, so both sides keep what they care about.

subtype: Approach: mixing two ideas into one plan [Thinking]
passage: In Nazia's flat in Pune, the four of them had been arguing since lunch. Binita and Nazia wanted a poster about the water cycle, with arrows and labels. A little plastic-cup cloud that tips and drips into a bottle-cap sea?" The boys looked at each other. "Moving part?" "Moving part." Nazia was already drawing the arrows.

subtype: Approach: dividing jobs by what each person is good at [Action]

Munni, who was never scared in front of the class, would present it. Nobody fought over the glue this time. The chart was done in two afternoons, and Munni's talk made Masterji clap.

subtype: Approach: dividing jobs by what each person is good at [Action]
passage: In Montevideo, Camila's group had a week to make a poster about the birds of their city park. The first meeting turned into an argument over who would hold the markers. qa.q: How might Mateo see his job?
qa.a: Mateo loves talking, so presenting likely feels like a fun job rather than a chore.

grounding: Illustrates a group dividing a project by what each member does best, which speeds up the work and cuts down on quarrels.
